idiom_name: discriminated-union command types + exhaustive typed dispatcher + async queue
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the closure-as-command idiom of JavaScript and adds a compile-time contract: model commands as a discriminated union on a `type` tag and the processor as a mapped handler record `{ [K in Command['type']]: (c: Extract<Command, { type: K }>) => Promise<Result> }`, so adding a command without its handler fails to compile and the dispatcher needs no casts. The queue is still an array/AsyncQueue (or an RxJS `Subject` with a `queueScheduler` when ordering and backpressure must be declarative), and undo is a stack of inverse functions. Classes remain worthwhile only where commands cross a trust or process boundary: there the union doubles as the wire schema, and runtime validation (zod, io-ts, class-validator) must re-check what the types erased.
pitfalls: Types vanish at runtime: commands arriving from HTTP/queues must be validated against a schema before dispatch, or an unknown tag reaches the handler map and throws.
`as never` (or a `default:` branch) silences the exhaustiveness guarantee the union was chosen for; keep the dispatcher generic instead of casting.
A persisted log of union-typed commands needs an explicit version tag per variant, otherwise replaying an older log against new code deserialises into the wrong handler.
Async handlers that mutate shared state without serialising per key race exactly as in plain JavaScript - the type system says nothing about interleaving.
